meta.title: Who really said "Pay no attention to the man behind the curtain"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: The Wizard says "that man," not "the man" — and Baum's 1900 novel has no curtain at all. Written by Langley, Ryerson & Woolf for MGM, 1939.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Pay no attention to the man behind the curtain'?
meta.ogDescription: It's "that man" — the demonstrative is the joke. And the line isn't Baum's: his novel has a screen, not a curtain. MGM's writers, 1939.

answer.label: Not quite — the actual line is “that man behind the curtain”
answer.authorName: Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson & Edgar Allan Woolf
answer.authorDates: Credited screenwriters, MGM's The Wizard of Oz (1939)
answer.sourceLine: In the film, the exposed Wizard (Frank Morgan) blusters “Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!” — the demonstrative is the joke, because he is pointing away from himself while standing in plain sight. The popular version smooths “that man” into the flatter “the man,” and the line is routinely credited to L. Frank Baum, whose 1900 novel contains no curtain at all.

source.excerpt:
[Toto pulls back the curtain, revealing the Wizard at the controls of the throne apparatus. Dorothy calls the others' attention to him.]

DOROTHY: Who are you?

OZ’S VOICE: Oh — I — Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain. Go — before I lose my temper! The Great and Powerful — Oz — has spoken!

[Dorothy pulls back the curtain to reveal the Wizard at the controls. He starts to speak into the microphone — then turns weakly back to Dorothy.]

DOROTHY: Who are you?

OZ’S VOICE: Well, I — I — I am the Great and Powerful — Wizard of Oz.
trail: The transcript. Wikiquote's page for the 1939 film ↗ transcribes the Wizard's dialogue as “Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!” and heads the page “Written by Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson, and Edgar Allan Woolf, based on the novel The Wonderful Wizard of Oz by L. Frank Baum.”

The production document. MGM's own cutting continuity, last revised 15 March 1939 ↗, independently records the same wording — “…attention to that man behind the curtain” — and carries the three writers' names on its title page. Two records, made independently, agree on the demonstrative.

The origination check. Searching the complete 1900 novel at Project Gutenberg ↗ returns no occurrence of “curtain” and none of “pay no attention.” Baum instead has Toto tip over “the screen that stood in a corner,” exposing “a little old man, with a bald head and a wrinkled face.” The film did not sharpen an existing line here — it invented one.

The authorship. Wikipedia's production history ↗ records that the credit is shared and that the script passed through at least ten writers, while Langley's biography ↗ details how Ryerson and Woolf revised his draft without his knowledge. We can name the three credited authors; we cannot honestly name which one wrote this sentence.
source.excerptNote: Reconstructed from MGM's cutting continuity, which records dialogue split across camera setups — the line is logged as “Oh — I — Pay no…” on one shot and “…attention to that man behind the curtain” on the next; the joins are ours, the words are not. One further precision: Wikiquote pairs the line with “The Great Oz has spoken!”, but in the continuity that exclamation lands a beat earlier, and what follows the curtain line is “The Great and Powerful — Oz — has spoken!”

source.rightsNote: The Wizard of Oz was released by MGM on 25 August 1939 — long after the 1931 threshold beyond which US works remain under copyright — so the film and its dialogue are firmly in copyright. Because screen writing is work-for-hire, the rights sit with the studio rather than with Langley, Ryerson or Woolf or their estates: Wikipedia records ↗ that home video releases are issued by Warner Home Video “via current rights holder Turner Entertainment Co.” Baum's 1900 novel is separately in the public domain, but the line quoted here is not from it.

author.name: Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson & Edgar Allan Woolf
author.heading: Who actually wrote it
author.metaLine: Credited screenwriters · The Wizard of Oz (MGM, 1939)
author.bio: The 1939 screenplay carries a shared credit: Noel Langley (1911–1980) wrote the script that formed the basis of the film, and it was then revised by the writing team of Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf — revisions Langley disliked enough that he stripped many of them back out when producer Arthur Freed returned the script to him. At least ten writers passed over the material without credit, among them George Cukor, King Vidor and Irving Brecher. Because the credit is shared and the drafts were heavily reworked, the surviving credit does not establish which of the three actually wrote this particular line — it establishes only that the line is theirs collectively, and not the actor's or the character's.

misattribution.heading: Three ways this one goes wrong
misattribution.intro: Nobody is falsely credited here — the film is real and the scene is real. Three things go wrong anyway: the wording, the origin, and the author.

items.why: The film says that man. Both Wikiquote's transcription of the released film ↗ and MGM's own cutting continuity of 15 March 1939 ↗ read “that man behind the curtain.” The swap looks trivial and isn't: the Wizard is pointing away from himself, and “that” is what makes it a deflection rather than a description.

items.who: L. Frank Baum / The Wonderful Wizard of Oz (1900)
items.why: The line is regularly credited to Baum's novel, on the reasonable assumption that a famous Oz line is an Oz line. It isn't. A full-text search of the 1900 novel at Project Gutenberg ↗ finds the word “curtain” zero times. Baum's Wizard sits behind a screen, which Toto knocks over when the Lion roars, and his first words are “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible” followed by a plea not to be struck. The curtain, the bluster and the sentence are all the film's.

Quote collections routinely file the line under the actor or the character. Frank Morgan performed it; the Wizard is a fictional person and cannot write anything. The words belong to the credited screenwriters — per Wikipedia's production history ↗, “the screenplay is credited to Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson, and Edgar Allan Woolf, but includes contributions from other writers.”

misattribution.truthLine: The real sentence is “Pay no attention to that man behind the curtain!” — written for MGM in 1939 under a shared credit to Noel Langley, Florence Ryerson and Edgar Allan Woolf, spoken by Frank Morgan, and nowhere in the book it is credited to ↗.

context.heading: Why the line stuck
lead: The line survives because it describes a manoeuvre with no dignity in it. The Wizard has already been seen — Toto has hauled the curtain aside, the control panel is in shot, the great floating head is revealed as a man working levers into a microphone — and rather than stop, he keeps the amplified voice running and instructs the room to disregard the evidence of its own eyes. He is not hiding. He is asking to be treated as though he were.

That is why the phrase migrated out of the film and into ordinary speech about politics, markets, monetary policy and public relations: it names the specific moment when a concealment has failed and the concealer brazens on anyway. The word the popular version drops is the one doing the work. That man is a man being pointed at. The man is a generic figure behind a generic curtain — the phrase becomes a comment about hidden power in general, which is roughly the opposite of the joke.
detailsBody: Baum's 1900 novel stages the exposure differently and less theatrically. The Cowardly Lion roars to frighten the Wizard; the roar startles Toto, who jumps aside and knocks over a screen standing in the corner. Behind it is “a little old man, with a bald head and a wrinkled face,” as surprised as they are, who says only: “I am Oz, the Great and Terrible — but don't strike me — please don't.”

There is no curtain, no bluster, and no attempt to talk his way out of it — Baum's Wizard folds immediately. The film's writers supplied the curtain, the failed brazen-out, and the line. The device of a concealed operator exposed by Toto is Baum's; the sentence people quote is not.
context.pull: He is not hiding. He is asking to be treated as though he were.
